case.presentation: Patient is a 40-year-old man with a history of multiple sports-related traumatic brain injuries who presents with two years of progressively worsening left-sided headaches. What began as occasional sharp stabbing pains every few months has evolved into 8-hour episodes occurring 2-3 days each week. These episodes interfere with work, and are accompanied by photophobia and infrequent nausea. He has no red flag symptoms (ie, focal findings) and uses aspirin and ibuprofen abortively. He has never seen a neurologist or had imaging. Should imaging be obtained? What treatments are recommended?
case.recommendations: The patient should have urgent MRI brain imaging with and without contrast before further symptomatic treatment to assess for a mass lesion or vascular lesion. Headaches following traumatic brain injury generally improve over time. The patient's worsening headaches are concerning. Without a neurologic exam, it is challenging to further determine urgency of the symptoms. The patient should be referred urgently to neurology. Given his frequent use of aspirin and ibuprofen, he should be warned about the risk of medication overuse headache as well.
